---
title: "Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
cal <- readRDS("data/calibration.rds")
rel <- cal$reliability
pt <- cal$metrics
ci <- cal$ci
raw_rel <- rel[rel$score == "Raw VendorScore", ]
top <- raw_rel[raw_rel$bin == max(raw_rel$bin), ]
n_under <- sum(raw_rel$observed > raw_rel$predicted)
vb <- cal$vendor_bands
wc <- cal$window_counts
fitw <- wc[wc$window == "calibration_fit", ]
evw <- wc[wc$window == "overlay_eval", ]
sgn <- function(x, d = 5) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f"))
dif <- function(v, m, d = 5) {
  r <- ci[ci$variant == v & ci$metric == m, ]
  sprintf("%s (%s to %s)", sgn(pt[v, m] - pt["Raw VendorScore", m], d), sgn(r$diff_low, d), sgn(r$diff_high, d))
}
ece_rows <- ci[ci$variant != "Raw VendorScore" & ci$metric %in% c("ece_mass", "ece_width"), ]
n_ece_zero <- sum(ece_rows$diff_low <= 0 & ece_rows$diff_high >= 0)
up_n <- sum(vb$move == "Moves up"); same_n <- sum(vb$move == "No change")
```

### The question

When VendorScore says a vendor has a 10% chance of an incident, do incidents happen about
10% of the time? RiskMetric Systems asserts that its scores are "well-calibrated." NorthPoint
cannot inspect the model, but it can compare the scores with what happened, and it can test
whether a recalibration overlay would help.

### Method in brief

VendorScore trained on months 1 to 30
(the vendor's business). We fitted the overlay on months 31 to 36
(`r format(fitw$vendor_months, big.mark = ",")` vendor-months, `r fitw$incidents` incidents), so the classifier had not trained on
those rows. Every result below comes from months 37 to 48 (`r format(evw$vendor_months, big.mark = ",")` vendor-months,
`r evw$incidents` incidents, `r evw$vendors` vendors), which nothing was fitted or selected on.

We fixed the methods before looking at that window: an isotonic overlay (a monotone curve,
interpolated between fitted points), and a Platt overlay (a logistic curve on the logit of
the score) as secondary. Both come from `probcal`.^[[`probcal`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=probcal) 0.2.0: `cal_isotonic()`, `cal_platt()`, `ece()` and `cal_test()`.]
The Brier score measures overall probability error, so it reflects more than calibration.
The expected calibration error (ECE) is the weighted average gap between score and outcome
across ten score groups; it depends on how groups are formed, so we show equal-size and
equal-width groups. Uncertainty comes from resampling whole vendor histories (1,000 draws),
because the same vendors recur every month. Intervals condition on the fitted overlay and
leave out overlay-fitting uncertainty.

### Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-reliability
#| fig-cap: "Reliability diagram, months 37–48. Filled points: observed rate with vendor-clustered 95% intervals. Open diamonds: mean true probability in the group."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, raw and isotonic-overlay scores, plotting observed incident rate against predicted probability on a square-root scale with a diagonal. Raw top group lies below the diagonal."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
rel2 <- rel[rel$score %in% c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay"), ]
rel2$score <- factor(rel2$score, levels = c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay"))
brk <- c(0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10)
ggplot(rel2, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high, colour = score), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score), size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = true_mean), shape = 5, colour = "grey25", size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~score) +
  scale_x_sqrt(breaks = brk, labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_y_sqrt(breaks = brk, labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("vermillion", "blue")]), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Average predicted probability (square-root scale)",
       y = "Observed incident rate (square-root scale)")
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each dot groups vendor-months with similar scores: left to right
is the prediction, bottom to top is what happened. A dot on the grey diagonal means the model
was right on average. The vertical line is a plausible range; the open diamond is the
true average risk, known only because the data are simulated.

**What the plot tells you.** In the raw panel, the top group is the clearest miss. Only 75
incidents lie behind these dots, so single-group intervals are wide.
:::

The raw top-scored group was told it faced `r pct(top$predicted)`; `r pct(top$observed)` had an incident
(interval `r pct(top$low)` to `r pct(top$high)`), and its true average risk was `r pct(top$true_mean)`. The observed rate exceeded the
score in `r n_under` of 10 groups, mostly low-scored ones. These intervals are pointwise, so
they do not amount to a global test. The isotonic overlay collapses tied scores into
`r max(rel$bin[rel$score == "Isotonic overlay"])` distinct groups, not ten.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration metrics, months 37–48. Changes are versus raw scores, with vendor-clustered 95% intervals."
tab <- data.frame(
  Scores = c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay", "Platt overlay (logit scale)", "Observed"),
  Brier = c(sprintf("%.5f", pt[, "brier"]), "—"),
  `Brier change vs raw` = c("—", dif("Isotonic overlay", "brier"),
                            dif("Platt overlay (logit scale)", "brier"), "—"),
  `ECE, equal-size groups` = c(sprintf("%.4f", pt[, "ece_mass"]), "—"),
  `ECE, equal-width groups` = c(sprintf("%.4f", pt[, "ece_width"]), "—"),
  `Incidents per month` = c(sprintf("%.1f", pt[, "expected_per_month"]),
                            sprintf("%.1f", cal$observed_per_month)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrrrrr")
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is a version of the scores; the last row is the actual
count. Smaller Brier and ECE are better. The "change" column shows how each overlay moves
Brier versus raw scores, with a plausible range in brackets. The last column is the
incidents per month the scores imply.

**What the table tells you.** Both overlays lower Brier slightly, but the isotonic range
includes zero and the Platt range only just excludes it. `r n_ece_zero` of the 4 ECE changes have
ranges that include zero. All three score versions imply fewer incidents (`r sprintf("%.1f", min(pt[, "expected_per_month"]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(pt[, "expected_per_month"]))` a
month) than the `r sprintf("%.1f", cal$observed_per_month)` observed.
:::

Overlay gains are small and statistically unclear. The raw count of `r sprintf("%.1f", pt["Raw VendorScore", "expected_per_month"])`
incidents a month is closest to what was observed. The true probabilities imply only
`r sprintf("%.1f", cal$p_true_per_month)`, so some shortfall is chance. Changing vendor mix,
thin calibration data and a six-month fitting window may all contribute; this exercise does
not isolate them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bands
#| fig-cap: "Vendors by risk band, raw versus isotonic-overlay scores (Low <1%, Medium 1–<3%, High ≥3% monthly probability; illustrative). A retrospective illustration."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart counting vendors that keep or change risk band under the isotonic overlay."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
mov <- cal$moves
mov$path <- factor(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to),
                   levels = unique(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to)[order(mov$move != "No change", mov$from)]))
ggplot(mov, aes(path, Freq, fill = move)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No change" = unname(okabe_ito["grey"]),
                               "Moves down" = unname(okabe_ito["blue"]),
                               "Moves up" = unname(okabe_ito["vermillion"]))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Risk band under raw → overlay scores", y = "Number of vendors", fill = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Vendors are put in Low, Medium or High risk bands using their
average score over months 37 to 48. These bands are separate from the criticality tiers of
vendors. Each bar counts vendors by band before and after the overlay.

**What the plot tells you.** `r same_n` of 300 vendors keep their band and `r up_n` move up; none move down.
This shows the overlay's decision impact, not that the new bands are right; averaging a
whole window is a retrospective device, not a monitoring rule.
:::

### So what

The vendor's calibration claim does not hold cleanly: the highest-risk group is overstated
and the overlay evidence is thin. Outcomes analysis (§V) can support an overlay (§VII), but
does not make one acceptable by itself. This one has not shown fitness for the use: Brier gains are small, ECE changes are
mostly indistinguishable from zero, and no operational acceptance threshold was set in
advance, so we do not invent one. This is a corrected retrospective demonstration, not a
prospective validation, and only partial validation: it cannot say why the scores are
miscalibrated or whether the proprietary method is conceptually sound.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Technical note: kernel calibration test (exploratory)

The kernel test in `probcal::cal_test()` on raw scores gives p = `r pval(cal$claim_test$p.value)`. It treats
rows as independent although vendors recur monthly, so we do not rely on it.
:::

### Actionable Insights

Sound practice suggests not approving the tested overlay for routine use yet: investigate
the shortfall, keep the existing process under documented controls, and validate any
replacement on later outcomes against tolerances set in advance. Include a reliability
diagram in every validation pack. The April 17, 2026 interagency [*Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management*](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13a.pdf)
(Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) refers to the bank's own established performance thresholds (§V).
